title: Unto Us Is Born a Son
description: The fourteenth-century carol "Puer nobis nascitur" from Piae Cantiones (1582), in G. R. Woodward's English words and the Rev. G. H. Palmer's harmony from The Cowley Carol Book, arranged for 2 to 4 singers. Verses 1, 2, 4 and 5 in D at a walking pace; the tune climbs from the low D to the high E and closes each verse by singing its last line twice.

credits.words: George Ratcliffe Woodward (The Cowley Carol Book, 1902), from the Latin "Puer nobis nascitur"
credits.arrangement: The Rev. G. H. Palmer's harmony (The Cowley Carol Book, 1902), adapted by Stackapella

licence.words: public domain: George Ratcliffe Woodward died 3 March 1934 (Wikipedia; Hymnary.org gives 1848-1934); his English words after the Latin carol, which the book heads "Words and tune (XIV Cent.) from Piae Cantiones", first printed in The Cowley Carol Book (1902, No. 25); sung as the 1912 impression prints them (old spellings and capitals kept: "Quires", "heav'n", "Owner", "Becradled"), verses 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the five, with verse 5's Latin lines ("Cum cantibus in choro", "Benedicamus Domino") as printed. The music repeats each verse's last line, as verse 1's underlay shows; the repeat is sung in every verse, with a comma after its first time. Verse 3 (Herod's slaughter of the children, the feast of the Holy Innocents) is left out: four verses keep the song a singable length, and verse 5, with its Latin, is the carol's close
licence.tune: public domain: the melody of "Puer nobis nascitur" from Piae Cantiones (Greifswald, 1582), traditional, as The Cowley Carol Book prints it, its editor G. R. Woodward died 1934
licence.arrangement: Palmer's organ harmony, signed "Harmony by Rev. G. H. Palmer" on the page (George Herbert Palmer died 20 June 1926; public domain), printed in four voices on two staves under a tune marked "To be sung in Unison": the alto, tenor and bass are its voices, read by stem direction (the alto the treble staff's down-stems, the tenor and bass the bass staff's up- and down-stems; a notehead stemmed both ways is both voices on one note), in his key and with his chords, fitted to the words one note a syllable and adapted for 2 to 4 beginners as follows. One note a syllable: Palmer's held and tied notes are sung again on each syllable (the alto's D4 through bar 1, the tenor's D4 on "of Quires", the bass's D3 on "Un-to us" and the bar-long D3, B2 and A2 of bars 4, 8 and 9); the tenor's dotted A3 and G3 quaver on "born a" and the alto's G4, F sharp 4, E4 on "per-" (a 4-3 suspension) become one note; on the tune's slur ("ter-", bar 8) the lower parts hold B3, F sharp 3 and B2 (his alto moves to C sharp 4); and on the last "ter-" they hold his D chord (his alto D4, B3 and tenor F sharp 3, G3 move under it), except in verse 5, where "Do-mi-no" has his G over D on "mi" (alto G4, tenor B3, bass D3). The alto takes each strong beat's third, for the duet: F sharp 4 and E4 on "Un-to" (his D4), so the song starts on a third above the tune's low D, not a unison, and crosses back under it through its E4; E4 and F sharp 4 on "a Son" (his C sharp 4, D4) and E4, F sharp 4, F sharp 4 on the last "e-ter-nal" (his C sharp 4, D4, B3, A3), stepping through the tune's E to a third above its closing low D, where Palmer doubles the D; F sharp 4 on "King of" (his D4) and on "per-" (his G4 suspension); F sharp 4 on the first "lords" (his D4); D4 on both "Lord"s (his C sharp 4), a D over A six-four into the A seventh, where his alto sat a bare fifth under the tune. The tenor takes the A chord's C sharp 4 on "a" and on the last "e-" (his A3 and G3: the alto has the E) and A3 on "Son" and the last "ter-nal" (his F sharp 3), so each cadence chord has root, third and fifth; it starts on A3 (his F sharp 3, which doubled the alto's new F sharp 4). The bass sings D3 on "King of" and the first "lords" (his F sharp 3 and F sharp 2), so the trio keeps the chord's root under the alto's F sharp; on the first "Of" the tenor and bass exchange his notes (tenor B3, bass D3; his D3, B2) so the bass's D3 into "lords" makes no fifths with the tune; B2 on "See" (his B3, over the bass's range) and D3 on the last "nal" (his D2, under it). Breaths written in for beginners: each line's last note gives up three quarters of a beat; "gun" and the first "nal" are crotchets, so they keep half a beat and the next line's "Of" starts a quarter beat late. Verse 4's "And O that Mary's gentle Child" has a syllable more than the tune's line, so "And O" share its first crotchet as two quavers in every part; verse 5 sings the book's own small crotchets in place of the minim for "cho-ro" (its "Let" then starts a quarter beat late, for the breath), takes the tune's slurred pair as "Do-mi" the first time, and splits the minim for the second "Do-mi". The duet and trio go without a third only on weak beats: the tune's passing E4 on "to", "a" and the last "e-" (the alto in unison with it on its way across), and Palmer's own chords where the alto sits a fourth, fifth or octave under the tune on a weak beat ("is", "be-", "His", "the", and the pickup "Of" before the last line, G over B with the alto D4, the trio having the bass's B2)
licence.source: The Cowley Carol Book for Christmas, Easter, and Ascension-tide, compiled and arranged by the Rev. G. R. Woodward, Revised and Enlarged Edition (London and Oxford: A. R. Mowbray & Co. Ltd., 1912; its preface dated Cadenabbia, Oct. 24, 1902), No. 25, "Unto us is born a Son", p. 37, "Puer nobis nascitur", "Words and tune (XIV Cent.) from Piae Cantiones. Harmony by Rev. G. H. Palmer", "To be sung in Unison", verse 1 under the music and verses 2 to 5 below it; in D major (two sharps), common time, in its printed key here; read from archive.org/details/cowleycarolbook0000grwo/page/n46 and checked note for note in every unclear place (the small crotchets in bars 2 and 4, the shared noteheads of bars 5 and 6) against the same plates in the 1922 impression, archive.org/details/cowleycarolbookf00wooduoft/page/n43. The book's Preface says the first issue of 39 carols came out in the autumn of 1901 and this revised and enlarged edition (65 carols) in 1902; Wikipedia ("Puer nobis nascitur") dates Woodward's translation to the Cowley Carol Book of 1902, No. 25
